title: Cleaning and restoring a tarnished silver-plated picture frame
subtitle: Remove tarnish from a silver-plated or gilded picture frame and restore the surface lustre
excerpt: How to clean a heavily tarnished silver-plated picture frame. Covers assessing the plating, removing tarnish with a silver polish or sodium bicarbonate method, cleaning the recesses, and protecting the restored finish with a wax barrier.
sourceNotes: Traditional silver care and metalwork cleaning practice. Period household management guides (pre-1928 public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin surface layer of silver sulphide (Ag2S) that forms when silver or silver-plated metal is exposed to hydrogen sulphide in the air. Tarnish appears as a yellow-to-black discolouration. It is a surface reaction only and does not damage the underlying silver; it can be removed without abrasion using a chemical reducing agent such as sodium bicarbonate and aluminium foil.

content.text: on a picture frame surface is removed chemically without abrasion. The electrochemical method (bicarbonate of soda with aluminium foil and hot water) converts the silver sulphide back to silver in minutes, without wearing away the plating. Abrasive silver polish also works but removes a thin layer of silver with each application and is less suitable for lightly plated pieces.

Examine the frame in good light. Areas where the silver plating has worn through to the base metal (usually a brass or copper coloured area) cannot be restored by cleaning; they would need replating. If the entire frame shows yellow or black tarnish but the silver surface beneath is intact, cleaning is the correct approach. Remove the glass and artwork from the frame before cleaning.

Line a bowl or sink with aluminium foil, shiny side up. Place the frame on the foil, ensuring the frame is in contact with the aluminium. Dissolve two tablespoons of bicarbonate of soda in two litres of boiling water and pour over the frame, ensuring the frame is submerged. A fizzing reaction will begin. The tarnish will begin to transfer from the silver to the aluminium within 5 to 10 minutes. Lift the frame out with tongs (not bare hands; the solution is hot), rinse with clean water, and dry immediately and thoroughly with a clean cloth.

Picture frame mouldings have deep recesses that retain tarnish after the electrochemical bath. Work a dry paintbrush (the 25 mm brush) into the recesses, using the bristles to lift and abrade any residual dark patches. A soft toothbrush is also effective in narrow channels. Follow with a cloth dampened with methylated spirit for any stubborn dark spots in deep recesses.

Once the frame is fully dry, apply a thin coat of clear microcrystalline wax or Renaissance wax to all silver surfaces using the paint brush. Buff with a clean cloth. The wax barrier slows future tarnishing by reducing the silver surface's exposure to air. Reapply annually in humid environments.

attrs.symptom: Frame retarnishes within weeks of cleaning
attrs.cause: No wax barrier applied, or the frame is stored in a high-humidity environment with wooden components (wood releases sulphur compounds that accelerate tarnishing).
attrs.fix: Apply a protective wax coat immediately after cleaning. Store cleaned silver pieces away from bare wood and wool textiles, which are the main sources of sulphur compounds in a domestic environment.

attrs.symptom: White residue appears on the moulding after the bicarbonate bath
attrs.cause: Undissolved bicarbonate deposits remaining in moulding recesses.
attrs.fix: Rinse thoroughly with clean warm water and brush out the recesses with a dry brush. The residue is harmless but should be removed before waxing.
